system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2174-08-01 15:05:00 to 2174-08-07 18:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with a two-day history of epigastric and mid-abdominal pain, nausea, and intolerance to oral intake, with symptoms reminiscent of a prior gastrojejunal ulcer. She was kept NPO initially, started on IV dextrose for glucose stability, and underwent an upper GI series that showed no leak, stricture, or obstruction. Tube feeds were restarted with Vivonex but poorly tolerated; she transitioned successfully to Jevity 1.5 at 45 mL/hr with improved tolerance. Erythromycin was added to enhance gastric motility, and her antiemetic was changed from ondansetron to prochlorperazine with good effect. She remained hemodynamically stable, achieved goal enteral nutrition, and was discharged home on a regimen of continuous and bolus tube feeding, erythromycin, and PRN prochlorperazine, with follow-up planned.
problems: Gastrojejunal ulcer, unspecified as acute or chronic, without hemorrhage or perforation
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

You were admitted to the hospital with esophageal burning. 
Therefore, you were given an IV medication to help protect your 
esophagus and stomach from acid and underwent an EGD to evaluate 
why you have such persistent acid reflux. Your EGD showed you 
have irritation of your stomach and esphagus and a narrowing of 
part of your digestive tract that makes it more likely for you 
to have reflux. Our GI team recommended you continue your 
antacid medications and try to position your body as upright as 
possible to optimize your stomach's chances of emptying. Your 
diet was advanced and you were tolerating increased oral intake 
well, so your tube feeds were decreased. You are now preparing 
for discharge to home with the following instructions:

Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner or return to the 
Emergency Department for any of the following:
*You experience new chest pain, pressure, squeezing or 
tightness.
*New or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or wheeze.
*If you are vomiting and cannot keep down fluids or your 
medications.
*You are getting dehydrated due to continued vomiting, diarrhea, 
or other reasons. Signs of dehydration include dry mouth, rapid 
heartbeat, or feeling dizzy or faint when standing.
*You see blood or dark/black material when you vomit or have a 
bowel movement.
*You experience burning when you urinate, have blood in your 
urine, or experience a discharge.
*Your pain in not improving within ___ hours or is not gone 
within 24 hours. Call or return immediately if your pain is 
getting worse or changes location or moving to your chest or 
back.
*You have shaking chills, or fever greater than 101.5 degrees 
Fahrenheit or 38 degrees Celsius.
*Any change in your symptoms, or any new symptoms that concern 
you.

Please resume all regular home medications, unless specifically 
advised not to take a particular medication. Also, please take 
any new medications as prescribed.

Please get plenty of rest, continue to ambulate several times 
per day, and drink adequate amounts of fluids.

Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery while taking narcotic 
pain medications.

We wish you a speedy recovery,
Your ___ Care Team
 
Followup Instructions:
___

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having a burning pain in your chest and upper belly for the past few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been really bad—like a fire moving up from my stomach into my throat. It feels just like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you didn’t stop your tube feeds before coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I kept them going. I only drank water by mouth. I didn’t want to make things worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve reviewed your history. You’ve had this kind of pain before, linked to reflux and ulcers after your gastric bypass reversal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. Last time, changing the feeding formula and starting erythromycin helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve started you on an IV medication—pantoprazole—to reduce stomach acid and protect your esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Is it safe to keep my tube feeds going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing them. We’re also increasing the rate a bit because your nutrition needs are high. We want to avoid another drop in your blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been worried about that too. The hypoglycemia scares me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring it closely. Your erythromycin is still running—it helps your stomach empty better, which should help with both reflux and sugar control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the cholestyramine? I’ve never taken that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It binds bile acids that can worsen reflux. It’s often helpful in cases like yours. We’ll give it twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. Should I be worried about the pain getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. We did an X-ray earlier—no blockage or free air. Your bowels look normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Do you think it’s another ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. The GI team wants to do an EGD—upper endoscopy—to check your stomach and the surgical connections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning. We’ll keep you comfortable until then. We also added prochlorperazine for nausea if it flares up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want this burning to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well during the EGD this morning. I have the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did it go? Did you see what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. There’s inflammation in your stomach—gastritis—and some small, healing ulcers near the surgical connection where your stomach meets the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not bleeding or perforated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the ulcers are clean-based, which means they’re not actively bleeding. There’s also a slight narrowing in your stomach anatomy that may be slowing emptying and contributing to reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why the burning keeps coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The GI team recommends staying on the pantoprazole, but now twice a day instead of once. We’ll also keep the sucralfate to coat the ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the erythromycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing it. It helps move things through. We’re also adding ranitidine at bedtime—it gives extra acid control overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I try eating anything by mouth now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips and soft foods. Your stomach needs time to heal. If you tolerate it, we’ll gradually increase.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your pain is much better, and you’ve kept down your oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the burning is mostly gone. I had some applesauce and broth yesterday with no problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to reduce your tube feeds back to your home rate since you’re eating more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I prefer to eat normally when I can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep supporting you. Your labs are stable—no anemia worsening, and your electrolytes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made steady progress. Pain is controlled, you’re tolerating a full stage 3 diet, and your bowel function is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge on Friday. We’ll make sure you have all your medications sorted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need new prescriptions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll take pantoprazole twice daily now, cholestyramine twice a day, and ranitidine at night. All your other meds stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your usual schedule—continuous overnight and bolus during the day as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your follow-up is set with Dr. Kim next week. They’ll monitor your ulcer healing and reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Should I sleep upright?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, elevate the head of your bed. It helps reduce nighttime reflux. Also avoid lying down right after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: you’re pain-free, eating well, and labs are stable. Discharge is tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. Thank you for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: call if the pain returns, or if you vomit blood, run a fever, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep taking all the meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your tube site looks great—no redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Keep resting, stay upright after meals, and follow up with Dr. Kim.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with a three-day history of epigastric and esophageal burning pain, similar to prior episodes linked to gastrojejunal ulcers and reflux. She remained on tube feeds throughout and was started on IV pantoprazole, cholestyramine, and continued erythromycin for gastric motility. An EGD revealed clean-based ulcers at the gastro-gastric anastomosis, gastric friability, and antral erythema consistent with gastritis. Her symptoms improved with increased acid suppression using pantoprazole twice daily, addition of ranitidine, and continuation of sucralfate. Oral intake was advanced successfully, tube feeds were reduced to baseline, and she was discharged home with medication adjustments and a follow-up appointment. She remained hemodynamically stable throughout, with no complications.
problems: Gastrojejunal ulcer, unspecified as acute or chronic, without hemorrhage or perforation
